I mean specifically the "fad diet" argument. I mean, sure, fasting works, but it's not really something you can do for a year, or many, is it?

Fasting, whether intermittent or prolonged, is rather easy. For an intermittent fast, one might break out of the eating window every now and then for social or medical reasons (for example, one's boss invites him to lunch, or a doctor prescribes something that should be taken with food, spread throughout the day), but one can then go right back to the plan with no problems.

Granted, fasting can be made difficult if one actively tries to eat at a caloric deficit (in which case, all of the troubles of simple caloric deficit diets kick in), or if one does not consume enough water, or if one tries to make a drastic change very quickly (note that the person to whom you link made incremental changes to shrink the eating window). But fasting in itself need not be difficult. And indeed, one can do it for a year, even if it is a prolonged fast:

Features of a successful therapeutic fast of 382 days' duration http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2495396/

I suppose that, if you really wanted to find an opener, you could talk about the commonalities between fasting and keto. Intermittent fasting is akin to low-carb eating generally, because both result in decreased insulin levels and thus greater burning of fat. And prolonged fasting results in ketosis, since not consuming any foods necessarily means not consuming any carbohydrates.

If someone who is doing keto or intermittent fasting hits a plateau, it could be helpful to recommend the other. That is, if keto doesn't seem to be enough for someone, recommend the addition of intermittent fasting. And if intermittent fasting doesn't seem to be enough, recommend keto, or perhaps even prolonged fasting. (The precise recommendations would depend on the specific case, of course.) Note that the person to whom you link writes about starting to "eat healthy (no dairy, no white flour, mostly fresh veggies and protein)". What makes 18 the special number (or 16)? I've been wondering this for a while, and reputable sources for this are rather difficult to find. The greatest cause seems (at least to me) likely to be linked with Piaget's developmental stages. In this model, he lists the final stage of human development as the "Formal Operational Stage". It ranges from 11 until 18ish. I've seen sources range it anywhere from 15 to 25 (and indefinitely). Then again, Piaget's work occurred during the 1900s (iirc the '30s), while laws forcing the age of adulthood being 16-18 began to form in the late 1800s in England, with the US quickly following. So this leaves me deeply confused. Why? I can totally understand it being related to Piaget, but the timeline doesn't seem consistent for that to be true.
Why was the age of adulthood bumped up to 16/17/18?

At 18 most people are done with high school or about to graduate. Therefore ready to enter the labor market as full time employees, or enter college, or both. In theory, if you are ready to work, you can sustain yourself, therefore you own your destiny. Having the adulthood age at 18 have economical implications, since that also the age in which you can enter the financial market and establish credit history, enter the housing market (most likely as renters), and be overall consumers. Also brain and behavioral development as Hank Green explains here.

As others have said or implied, this isn't a scientific question - it's a cultural one. Human adulthood is defined in myriad ways across different cultures and time periods. It isn't a scientific classification at all.

If you go into the human development literature, a scientific literature, you won't find anybody asking the scientific question: when does a person become a fully grown adult? You'll find people researching questions about different aspects of the developmental process - when does the adolescent growth spurt end? When do bones reach their maximal length, and what causes this? At what age have all the structures and functions of the adult brain taken shape? What environmental factors influence all of the above? And so on.

There are many relevant scientific questions to the cultural question of how to define adulthood. But adulthood is not a scientific classification in the sense you mean.
